title: Rich Rebuilds' ex-Hertz Polestar 2: a 'damaged' write-off that needed a battery charge and a $12 valve
dek: Rich Benoit bought a non-running 2023 Polestar 2 with about 80,000 miles from Hertz's salvage sell-off for about $3,000 and had it doing 0 to 60 in 3.9 seconds.

car.trim: Dual Motor, all-wheel drive; ex-rental with about 80,000 miles

source.where: A Hertz salvage auction, part of Hertz's EV sell-off; the auction house isn't named in the coverage
source.boughtNote: The video's title says $2,000; reports on it give about $2,900 paid and $3,125 with fees [2][3]. We use $3,125 as the figure that includes fees.
source.title: unknown
source.damage: Sold as not running and written off for alleged severe undercarriage damage. Benoit found a dead 12-volt battery, low coolant from a leaking coolant part, cooling fault codes, a snapped rear shock and a broken plastic splash shield; the high-voltage pack was undamaged [2][3].

episodes.t: I Bought a Banned Chinese Car From a Rental Company for $2,000
episodes.what: Benoit buys the dead ex-Hertz Polestar 2, finds the undercarriage damage was overstated, fixes a coolant leak and a dead 12-volt battery and runs 0 to 60 in 3.9 seconds.

parts.why: A faulty $12 plastic valve was leaking coolant and setting cooling-system faults [3].
The system was low from the leak [2].
It was dead, which is part of why the car wouldn't run; reports say it was charged, not replaced [2][3].

parts.part: JB Weld on a snapped rear shock absorber
parts.why: A temporary fix to get the car driving; a proper shock is still due [3].
The only broken underbody part he found; reports call it small and cheap [3].

time: One video, posted October 20, 2026: bought, diagnosed, fixed and tested in the same episode. No shop hours given.

costs.note: The $3,125 with fees is reported from the video; the title's $2,000 is lower. The $12 valve is stated; coolant ($30) and the JB Weld ($10) are our estimates. A proper rear shock and the splash shield aren't counted. Labor is his own.

value.basis: Clean, low-mileage 2023 Polestar 2 Long Range Dual Motors (11,000 to 29,000 miles) are listed at dealers for about $23,400 to $27,400 [4]. This one has about 80,000 miles, a rental history, a snapped shock and an insurance write-off that is likely to brand its title, so our estimate is roughly half or less.

verdict: It paid, quickly. About $3,200 in, by our count, bought a running, nearly 500-horsepower EV that Benoit timed at 3.9 seconds to 60 and that would still fetch several times that even with 80,000 miles and a branded title. The real lesson is about the listing: a car written off for severe undercarriage damage had a dead 12-volt battery and a $12 valve. Fleet sell-offs move fast and inspect little, and someone who can diagnose an EV gets paid for it.
body:
## The buy

Rich Benoit, the Massachusetts YouTuber behind Rich Rebuilds, bought a non-running 2023 Polestar 2 from a Hertz salvage auction [1][3]. Hertz has been selling off a large share of its EV fleet, Teslas and Polestars among them [3]. The car is a dual-motor, all-wheel-drive Polestar 2 with about 80,000 rental miles [2][3].

The price depends on whose count you use. Benoit's video title says $2,000 [1]. Reporting on the video says he paid about $2,900, and $3,125 with fees [2][3]. We use $3,125, since it includes the fees.

The video calls the Polestar a "banned Chinese car," because the car and many of its parts are built in China [1][2]. That's a joke, not a legal point: Hertz told MotorBiscuit the Polestar 2 is not banned in the U.S. and existing cars are legal to own, buy and sell [3].

## The damage

Hertz's listing said the car had severe undercarriage damage, and that is why it was written off [2][3]. Benoit found none to speak of: the high-voltage battery pack was undamaged and the only broken underbody part was a small, cheap plastic splash shield [3]. He told viewers, as MotorBiscuit quotes him, "The undercarriage damage was a complete lie" [3].

What actually kept the car off the road was smaller. The 12-volt battery was dead, the coolant was low, and the car was throwing cooling-system fault codes [2]. The cause was a coolant leak at a pump: VT describes a cracked hose, and MotorBiscuit says it was a faulty $12 plastic valve [2][3]. A rear shock absorber had also snapped [3].

## The work and the parts

The fixes were cheap. He charged the 12-volt battery, topped up the coolant and replaced the leaking part [2][3]. The snapped shock got a temporary JB Weld repair, and the cheap replacement tires the car came with stayed on [3]. VT reports that the car still wouldn't go into drive right after the coolant repair, and doesn't say what finally fixed it [2]; MotorBiscuit doesn't mention the problem [3]. By the end of the episode it was driving.

Then he tested it. The car fast-charged at over 100 kW with no visible leaks, and ran 0 to 60 in 4.1 seconds and then 3.9 seconds [2][3]. Benoit said the car "still held up extremely well, was pretty dang reliable" after a rental life [3].

## The money

In: $3,125 with fees, plus the $12 valve, plus our estimates of about $30 for coolant and $10 for the JB Weld, for about $3,177. Benoit himself put it at about $3,500 for a 500-horsepower car under four seconds [3]. A proper rear shock and the splash shield are still to buy, and neither is priced in the coverage.

Out: low-mileage, clean 2023 Polestar 2 Long Range Dual Motors are listed at dealers for about $23,400 to $27,400 [4]. This car has 80,000 miles, a rental past, a temporary shock fix and an insurance write-off, which in most states brands the title, though its title hasn't been reported. We put it at $9,000 to $15,000. Even at the bottom of that range it is three times what he paid.

## What's next

A real shock and the splash shield, and then a choice: keep it, sell it, or use it as Rich Rebuilds' argument about Chinese-built cars, which is what the video was really for. On the numbers, this is one of the quickest wins in the garage.
